title: Scaling and Mise en Place
bigQuestion: How do you take a recipe written for one table and cook it, on time and without surprises, for a different table?

story.title: Forty Plates from a Recipe for Eight
story.kicker: The reunion was Saturday, the rice pilaf recipe fed eight, and Nia's cousin had already texted that forty people were coming.
paragraphs: The recipe card was in Nia's grandmother's handwriting: Rice Pilaf, serves 8. Two cups of rice, 4 cups of chicken broth, 3 tablespoons of oil, 1 onion, 1 teaspoon of salt, half a teaspoon of pepper. It took 30 minutes. Nia had made it twice. But forty people were not eight people, and her mother had put her in charge of the rice while the grown-ups handled the meat.

She started with one number. Forty divided by eight was five. Every amount on the card would be multiplied by five. Ten cups of rice. Twenty cups of broth. Fifteen tablespoons of oil. Five onions. Five teaspoons of salt. Two and a half teaspoons of pepper. She wrote the new list on a clean sheet and taped it next to the old card so she could see both.

Then the units started to fight her. Nobody measures fifteen tablespoons of oil one at a time. Sixteen tablespoons is a cup, so fifteen was a cup minus one, or 3/4 cup plus 3 tablespoons. Five teaspoons of salt was 1 tablespoon plus 2 teaspoons. Twenty cups of broth was five quarts, which was a gallon jug and one more quart carton. And ten cups of rice plus twenty cups of broth was thirty cups going into a pot before the rice even swelled. Her mother's biggest pot held 8 quarts, or 32 cups. "That is too close," her mother said. "Use two pots."

Saturday morning, Nia set up before she turned on a burner. Two pots on the stove. Five onions peeled and diced into one bowl. Rice measured into a second bowl, split in half. Broth poured into two pitchers. Salt and pepper in two little dishes, one per pot. Oil in a liquid cup. A timer. A wooden spoon for each pot. It looked like a cooking show, and that was the point: when the oil got hot, she would not be hunting for an onion.

The pilaf came out right, both pots, and the cousins ate all of it. That night Nia wrote three things on the back of the reunion recipe. The factor. The unit conversions. And, in capital letters, TWO POTS. The next time forty people came, the card would already know.
story.think: Nia did all her math before she cooked, not during. What would have gone wrong if she had multiplied each ingredient in her head while the oil was heating?

lessons.title: Parts of a Recipe
lessons.mainIdea: A written recipe has a yield, an ingredient list in order of use, and numbered steps; each part answers a different question before you cook.
reading: Lay a recipe on the counter and find its parts. The title tells you what it makes. The *yield* tells you how much: serves 8, makes 24 cookies, one 9-inch pie. The times tell you prep time, cook time and total time. The *ingredient list* names each item, its amount, and often how it is prepared: 1 onion, diced; 2 Tbsp butter, melted. The *method* is the numbered steps. Some recipes also list equipment and an oven temperature at the top.

The order of the ingredient list is not random. A well-written recipe lists ingredients in the order you use them, so the list is also a checklist. If butter is first and eggs are second, the first step will almost certainly cream the butter and then beat in the eggs. Read the list against the steps once, and you will catch a missing ingredient or a step that never uses something you set out.

The words after the comma matter as much as the amount. 1 cup walnuts, chopped means measure a cup of whole walnuts and then chop them. 1 cup chopped walnuts means chop first and then measure a cup. Those are different amounts of walnuts. The same goes for 1 cup flour, sifted against 1 cup sifted flour. Read the comma as an instruction about when to do the prep, and you will measure what the writer meant.

words.d: how much a recipe makes: number of servings, pieces or pans
the part of a recipe that names each item with its amount and its prep, usually in order of use
the numbered steps of a recipe, in the order you do them

look.title: Find the Parts
look.text: Oatmeal Cookies. Makes 24. Prep 15 min, bake 12 min. Oven 350 °F. 1 cup butter, softened; 1 cup packed brown sugar; 2 eggs; 1 tsp vanilla; 1 1/2 cups flour; 1 tsp baking soda; 1/2 tsp salt; 3 cups rolled oats; 1 cup raisins. Step 1: Cream butter and sugar. Step 2: Beat in eggs and vanilla. Step 3: Stir in flour, soda and salt. Step 4: Stir in oats and raisins. Step 5: Drop by tablespoons; bake 12 minutes.
look.prompt: Name the yield, the times, the oven temperature, and the first ingredient used. Which ingredient list line tells you to do something before measuring?

check.q: What does the yield of a recipe tell you?
choices: How long it takes to cook
What temperature to set the oven
check.why: Yield is the amount produced: serves 8, makes 24 cookies. It is the number you scale from.

check.q: What is the difference between 1 cup walnuts, chopped and 1 cup chopped walnuts?
choices: The first is measured whole and then chopped; the second is chopped and then measured
The second means walnut pieces from a bag
check.why: The comma tells you the prep comes after measuring. Chopped nuts pack closer, so the two lines give different amounts.

check.q: Why do good recipes list ingredients in the order they are used?
choices: So the most expensive item is first
So the list doubles as a checklist that matches the steps
check.why: Order of use lets you check the list against the steps and catch anything missing before you start.

lessons.title: Read It Twice Before You Start
lessons.mainIdea: Read the whole recipe before touching anything, once for the picture and once for the numbers, tools and waiting times.
reading: The most common recipe disaster is not a bad measurement. It is step 6 saying chill the dough for 2 hours when dinner is in 45 minutes. Read the whole recipe before you do anything. The first pass is for the picture: what is this food, what does it look like at the end, and roughly how does it get there? The second pass is for the details: every number, every tool, every place the recipe makes you wait.

On the second pass, hunt for hidden time. Softened butter means it has been out of the refrigerator for a while. Marinate overnight, let rise until doubled, cool completely before frosting: each of these is a clock you cannot skip. Hunt for hidden tools: a 9-by-13 pan, a wire rack, a thermometer, a blender. Hunt for hidden ingredients in the steps that are not in the list, like the water for boiling pasta or the oil for the pan.

Then check what you have. Open the refrigerator and the cabinet and touch each ingredient. Two eggs on the card means two eggs in the carton. If something is missing, now is the time to decide: substitute, borrow, or pick a different recipe. Carpenters say measure twice, cut once. In a kitchen it is read twice, cook once. The five minutes you spend reading will save you the twenty you would spend fixing.

words.d: the time to measure, chop and get ready before the heat goes on
waiting built into a recipe, like chilling, rising, marinating or cooling, that is not in the cook time

look.title: Measure Twice
look.cite: traditional carpenter's proverb, English, origin unknown
look.prompt: Rewrite this proverb for the kitchen. What is the kitchen version of measuring twice, and what is the cut you cannot undo?

check.q: Dinner is in 45 minutes. A student picks a chicken recipe that says marinate 4 hours. When should this have been caught?
choices: After the chicken was in the marinade
When the family sat down to eat
During the second read of the recipe, before starting
check.why: Reading the whole recipe first turns up hidden waiting time before anything is started.

check.q: Which of these is hidden time in a recipe?
choices: Let the dough rise until doubled, about 1 hour
check.why: Rising is waiting that is not counted in cook time. Baking is cook time; the others are not time at all.

check.q: What is the point of touching each ingredient in the refrigerator and cabinet before you start?
choices: To find out what is missing while you can still substitute or change plans
To put them in alphabetical order
check.why: Finding a missing ingredient before you begin gives you choices. Finding it halfway through does not.

lessons.title: Mixing Words
lessons.mainIdea: Cream, beat, whisk, stir and fold are different motions with different results; a recipe picks one on purpose.
reading: A recipe says cream the butter and sugar, and a student stirs them together for ten seconds with a spoon. The cookies come out flat and dense. To *cream* means to beat softened butter and sugar together with a mixer or a strong arm until the mix turns pale and fluffy, 2 to 3 minutes. The sugar crystals cut tiny air pockets into the fat, and those pockets are what make cookies and cakes light. Ten seconds with a spoon does not make any pockets.

*Beat* means to mix hard and fast, with a spoon, whisk or mixer, until smooth. *Whisk* means to beat with a wire whisk, which adds air; you whisk eggs, and you whisk dry ingredients together to blend them. *Stir* is gentler: a spoon moving in circles until the ingredients are combined and no more. Stir in the chocolate chips means just until they are spread through the dough.

*Fold* is the gentlest of all. You fold when one ingredient is full of air, like beaten egg whites or whipped cream, and the recipe does not want that air knocked out. Use a rubber spatula. Cut down through the middle of the bowl, sweep along the bottom, and bring the batter up and over the top. Turn the bowl a quarter turn and repeat. Stop as soon as the streaks disappear. Stirring or beating at this step deflates the mix, and a soufflé or an angel food cake will come out low and heavy.

words.d: to beat softened fat and sugar together until pale and fluffy, 2 to 3 minutes, to trap air
to mix hard and fast with a spoon, whisk or mixer until smooth
to beat with a wire whisk, adding air, as with eggs or to blend dry ingredients
to combine gently with a spatula, cutting down and turning over, so a light mixture keeps its air

look.title: Which Motion?
look.text: A recipe for a lemon cake has these steps: (1) butter and sugar until pale and fluffy; (2) eggs one at a time until smooth; (3) flour, baking powder and salt in a separate bowl until blended; (4) dry ingredients into the wet just until combined; (5) beaten egg whites into the batter without losing the air. The verbs have been left out.
look.prompt: Put the right mixing word on each step, name the tool for each, and say what goes wrong if step 5 is done with a mixer.

check.q: A recipe says to cream the butter and sugar. What should the mixture look like when you are done?
choices: Grainy and yellow, mixed for a few seconds
Pale and fluffy, after 2 to 3 minutes of beating
check.why: Creaming beats air into the fat with the sugar. It takes a few minutes and the mixture turns lighter in color.

check.q: Which motion is right for adding beaten egg whites to a batter?
choices: Beat with a mixer on high
Stir hard with a wooden spoon
Whisk fast in a wide bowl
Fold gently with a rubber spatula until the streaks disappear
check.why: Folding keeps the air in the whites. Beating or stirring knocks it out, and the cake comes out heavy.

check.q: Stir in the chocolate chips means to mix them
choices: just until they are spread through the dough
by folding them under egg whites
check.why: Stir is a gentle mix until combined. Overmixing at this point toughens the dough.

lessons.title: Heat Words
lessons.mainIdea: Simmer, boil, sauté and sear name how hot the pan is and how fast the food moves; each has a look you can recognize.
reading: Put a pot of water on the stove and watch it. First a few small bubbles form on the bottom and rise slowly, and the surface barely moves. That is a *simmer*. Next the bubbles come faster and break the surface all over, and the water rolls. That is a *boil*. Water boils at 212 °F at sea level, and no amount of extra heat makes it hotter; it just boils harder. Soups, beans and sauces usually simmer, because a hard boil breaks food apart and boils away the liquid. Pasta and potatoes boil.

*Sauté* comes from a French word for jump. You cook small pieces of food in a little fat over medium-high heat, moving them often, in a wide pan. The onions in Nia's pilaf were sautéed until soft and golden. *Sear* is hotter and stiller: a piece of meat goes into a very hot pan with a little oil and sits without moving until a brown crust forms, then turns once. Crowding the pan with too much food drops the temperature, and instead of browning, the food steams in its own juice and turns gray.

Two more words show up in ovens. *Bake* is dry heat all around the food, usually 325 to 400 °F for cakes, breads and casseroles. *Roast* is the same dry heat, usually hotter, for meat and vegetables, so the outside browns. Whatever the word, the oven must reach its temperature before the food goes in, which takes 10 to 15 minutes. Turn it on first. The recipe says preheat because a cake that goes into a cold oven spreads before it sets.

words.d: to cook in liquid just below a boil, with small slow bubbles and a barely moving surface
to cook in liquid at 212 °F at sea level, with big fast bubbles that break the surface all over
to cook small pieces quickly in a little fat over medium-high heat, moving them often
to brown the outside of food in a very hot pan without moving it, then turn once
to turn the oven on ahead of time so it reaches the recipe's temperature before the food goes in

look.title: Look at the Pot
look.text: Four pans on a stove. Pan A: water with a few small bubbles rising slowly, surface calm, a pot of beans in it. Pan B: water rolling hard with big bubbles, pasta tossing in it. Pan C: a wide skillet, a little oil shimmering, diced onions moving as a student stirs. Pan D: a heavy skillet, very hot, one chicken thigh sitting still, a brown crust forming on the bottom, then a second student adds five more thighs at once.
look.prompt: Name the heat word for each pan. What is about to go wrong in Pan D, and what is the fix?

check.q: A soup recipe says simmer 20 minutes. What should the pot look like?
choices: Big bubbles rolling and breaking all over the surface
Small bubbles rising slowly with a barely moving surface
No bubbles at all, steam only
Bubbles only at the edge of a cold pot
check.why: Simmering is just below a boil. A rolling boil is too hard for soups and breaks the food apart.

check.q: At sea level, at what temperature does water boil?
check.why: Water boils at 212 °F at sea level. Higher heat just makes it boil harder, not hotter.

check.q: A student adds six chicken thighs to a hot skillet at once. They turn gray instead of brown. Why?
choices: The pan was overcrowded, so the temperature dropped and the meat steamed
check.why: Too much food at once cools the pan. The meat releases juice and steams instead of searing. Cook in batches.

lessons.title: Finding the Factor
lessons.mainIdea: Divide the servings you want by the servings the recipe makes; that number is the factor you multiply every ingredient by.
reading: Every scaled recipe starts with one number. The *factor* is the yield you want divided by the yield you have. Nia wanted 40 servings from a recipe for 8: 40 divided by 8 is 5. A recipe for 12 cookies that you want to make into 36: 36 divided by 12 is 3. A recipe for 6 that you want to cut to 3: 3 divided by 6 is 1/2. The factor can be a whole number, a fraction or a decimal, and every single ingredient gets multiplied by the same one.

Write the factor at the top of a clean sheet and work down the ingredient list one line at a time. Do not do it in your head at the stove. For factor 5: 2 cups rice becomes 10 cups; 1 tsp salt becomes 5 tsp; 1/2 tsp pepper becomes 2 1/2 tsp. For factor 1/2: 2 1/4 cups flour becomes 1 1/8 cups; 3/4 cup sugar becomes 3/8 cup; 2 eggs become 1 egg. Check each line twice. A single wrong line, like doubling the salt but not the rice, ruins a pot for forty.

Factors that are not whole numbers take care. A recipe for 8 that you want for 12 has a factor of 12 divided by 8, which is 1 1/2, or 1.5. Two thirds of a cup times 1.5 is 1 cup. One quarter teaspoon times 1.5 is 3/8 teaspoon, which you measure as 1/4 tsp plus 1/8 tsp. If an amount comes out awkward, round to the nearest thing you can measure, but never round salt, leavening or hot pepper up. Those are the ingredients where a little extra is a lot.

words.d: the number you multiply every ingredient by when scaling: servings wanted divided by servings the recipe makes
to change a recipe's amounts up or down so it makes more or less, using one factor for every ingredient

look.title: Pilaf for Forty, Factor 5
look.cite: example: a pilaf recipe for 8 (2 c rice, 4 c broth, 3 Tbsp oil, 1 onion, 1 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp pepper) scaled by 5
look.prompt: Check each row against the original recipe. Which rows would you rewrite in bigger units before you cook, and what would they become?

check.q: A recipe serves 6. You need to serve 18. What is the factor?
check.why: 18 divided by 6 is 3. Multiply every ingredient by 3.

check.q: A recipe for 8 is being scaled to 12. It calls for 2/3 cup of milk. How much milk now?
check.why: The factor is 12 divided by 8, or 1.5. Two thirds times 1.5 is 1 cup.

check.q: Which ingredient should you never round up when a scaled amount is awkward?
check.why: Salt, leavening and hot pepper are strong in small amounts. Round them down or measure exactly, never up.

lessons.title: Scaling Up and Changing Units
lessons.mainIdea: After multiplying, convert awkward amounts to bigger units with the equivalents chart, and check that your pot is big enough.
reading: Multiplying is half the job. The other half is turning 15 tablespoons and 20 cups into amounts you can actually measure. Use the chart. 16 Tbsp = 1 cup, so 15 Tbsp of oil is 3/4 cup plus 3 Tbsp. 3 tsp = 1 Tbsp, so 5 tsp of salt is 1 Tbsp plus 2 tsp. 4 cups = 1 quart, so 20 cups of broth is 5 quarts; that is a gallon jug plus one quart carton. Write the converted amount next to the multiplied one so both are on the sheet.

Then think about the pot and the pan. Ten cups of rice and twenty cups of broth is 30 cups before the rice swells, and an 8-quart pot holds 32 cups. That is too full to stir safely, and rice needs room. Split it into two pots. Baking has the same problem in a different shape: a doubled cake batter does not fit one 9-inch pan, and a batter twice as deep in the same pan will not bake in the same time. Use two pans of the recipe's size and keep the baking time.

Some things do not scale by the factor. Cooking time is one. Five times the rice in two pots takes about the same time as one pot, not five times as long, though a much bigger pot takes longer to come to a simmer. Pan size is another. Spices and salt are a third: a big pot often needs a little less than the factor says, so multiply, then taste before the last addition. Seasoning goes in near the end, when you can still fix it.

words.d: to multiply a recipe by a factor greater than 1 so it makes more
how much a pot or pan holds; an 8-quart pot holds 32 cups
one recipe's worth cooked at a time; a big scaled recipe is often cooked in several batches or pots

look.title: Will It Fit?
look.text: A chili recipe for 6 calls for 1 lb ground beef, 1 onion, 2 cans (15 oz each) of beans, 1 can (28 oz) crushed tomatoes, 2 cups water, 2 Tbsp chili powder, 1 tsp salt. A club is cooking for 30. The kitchen has one 8-quart pot and one 12-inch skillet.
look.prompt: Find the factor and scale each line. Convert the water to quarts and the chili powder to cups. Will it fit the pot? What is the safe minimum internal temperature for the ground beef, and how would you brown 5 pounds of it in one skillet?

check.q: After scaling, a recipe needs 15 Tbsp of oil. What is the easiest way to measure it?
check.why: 16 Tbsp = 1 cup, so 12 Tbsp = 3/4 cup, and 15 Tbsp is 3/4 cup plus 3 more tablespoons.

check.q: A recipe is scaled by 5 and needs 20 cups of broth. How much is that?
check.why: 4 cups = 1 quart, so 20 cups is 5 quarts. Four of those quarts make a gallon, leaving one more quart.

check.q: A cake recipe is doubled. What is the right choice for the pan?
choices: Pour all the batter into one pan and bake twice as long
Use two pans of the recipe's size and keep the baking time
Use one pan and lower the oven temperature
Use a bigger pan and bake at a higher temperature
check.why: Doubling the depth changes the baking time and the result. Two pans of the original size bake as the recipe was tested.

lessons.title: Scaling Down
lessons.mainIdea: Cutting a recipe uses a fraction as the factor; the tricky lines are eggs and small amounts of leavening.
reading: A cookie recipe makes 48 and you want 24: factor 1/2. A recipe for 12 servings for a family of 4: factor 1/3. Cutting down uses the same rule as scaling up, one factor for every line, but the amounts get awkward faster. Half of 2 1/4 cups flour is 1 1/8 cups, which is 1 cup plus 2 Tbsp. Half of 3/4 cup sugar is 3/8 cup, which is 6 Tbsp. Half of 1 tsp baking soda is 1/2 tsp. Half of 1/4 tsp is 1/8 tsp, and most spoon sets have that one.

Eggs are the hard line. Half of 2 eggs is 1 egg, easy. Half of 1 egg is not. Crack the egg into a small bowl, beat it with a fork until yolk and white are blended, and measure out about 2 tablespoons; that is close to half of a large egg. Half of 3 eggs is 1 1/2: use 1 whole egg plus about 2 Tbsp of a second beaten egg. Or change your factor so the eggs come out even: a recipe with 3 eggs cuts to 2/3 more cleanly than to 1/2.

Small amounts of leavening cannot be measured below 1/8 teaspoon, and a third of 1/4 tsp is no spoon anyone owns. In that case use the closest spoon you have and accept a small difference, or scale by a factor that keeps the leavening measurable. Cutting the pan size matters too. A half batch of brownies in the full 9-by-13 pan will be thin and overbake; use an 8-inch square pan, which holds close to half. Keep the oven temperature the same and start checking a few minutes early.

words.d: to multiply a recipe by a factor less than 1, such as 1/2 or 1/3, so it makes less
about 2 tablespoons of a large egg beaten in a bowl until the yolk and white are blended

look.title: Half a Batch
look.text: Chocolate chip cookies, makes 48: 2 1/4 cups flour, 1 tsp baking soda, 1 tsp salt, 1 cup butter, 3/4 cup sugar, 3/4 cup packed brown sugar, 1 tsp vanilla, 2 eggs, 2 cups chocolate chips. A student wants to make 24 cookies.
look.prompt: Write the half recipe. Give each amount in the easiest measure to use, including how many sticks of butter and how many tablespoons of sugar.

check.q: Half of 3/4 cup of sugar is
check.why: 3/4 cup is 12 Tbsp. Half of that is 6 Tbsp, or 3/8 cup.

check.q: A recipe calls for 1 egg and you are cutting it in half. What do you do?
choices: Beat the egg in a bowl and use about 2 tablespoons
check.why: A blended large egg is about 4 tablespoons, so about 2 tablespoons is half. Yolk or white alone changes the recipe.

check.q: A half batch of brownies goes into the full 9-by-13 pan at the recipe's time and temperature. What happens?
choices: They come out thin and overbaked
They come out too thick and raw in the middle
They will not rise at all
check.why: Half the batter in the same pan is half as deep, so it bakes through much faster and dries out. Use a smaller pan.

lessons.title: Everything in Its Place
lessons.mainIdea: Mise en place means every ingredient measured and every tool set out before the heat goes on, so cooking is only cooking.
reading: Watch a restaurant cook before the dinner rush. Small containers of diced onion, minced garlic, measured spices and chopped herbs sit in a row at the station. The pans are stacked, the tongs are in reach, the oil is in a squeeze bottle. That is *mise en place*, French for put in place. Every ingredient is measured and prepped, every tool is out, before a single burner is lit. When an order comes in, the cook only cooks.

In a home kitchen or a class lab, it looks like this. Read the recipe. Set out the pans and tools it names. Wash your hands for 20 seconds. Then go down the ingredient list in order, measuring each one into its own small bowl or onto a plate, doing the prep the comma asks for: dice the onion, soften the butter, beat the egg. Group things that go into the pan together in one bowl. Line the bowls up in the order they are used. Only now do you turn on the heat.

The reason is the clock. Sautéing onions takes about 5 minutes and garlic burns in 30 seconds. If you are still mincing garlic when the onions are done, the onions burn while you finish or the garlic goes in late. With everything measured, your hands are free to stir, watch and taste. Mise en place also catches mistakes early: you discover the missing egg at the counter, not with the batter half mixed. It looks slow. It is the fastest way to cook.

words.d: French for put in place: every ingredient measured and prepped and every tool set out before cooking starts
the work done to an ingredient before it is cooked: washing, peeling, chopping, measuring
the work area where a cook sets up tools and prepped ingredients

look.title: Two Cooks, One Stir-Fry
look.text: Recipe: heat oil, add onion 3 minutes, add garlic 30 seconds, add chicken until 165 °F, add sauce. Cook A has every ingredient in bowls lined up on the counter before turning on the burner. Cook B turns on the burner, adds oil, then starts slicing the onion, then looks for the garlic, then opens the chicken.
look.prompt: Walk through the first four minutes for each cook. What does Cook B's pan look like when the garlic finally goes in? Where does Cook B first fall behind?

check.q: What does mise en place mean in practice?
choices: Measuring and prepping every ingredient and setting out every tool before the heat goes on
Setting the table before guests arrive
check.why: Mise en place is the setup: everything measured, prepped and in reach, so cooking is only cooking.

check.q: A recipe adds garlic 30 seconds after the onions. Why must the garlic be minced before the onions go in?
choices: Garlic needs to rest before cooking
The onions need the garlic's flavor first
There is no time to mince it once the onions are cooking, and it burns fast
check.why: Thirty seconds is not enough time to mince garlic. With it prepped, it goes in on time and the onions do not burn while you wait.

check.q: Which is the correct order for a lab?
choices: Turn on the burner, then read the recipe, then measure
Measure while cooking, then wash hands at the end
Read the recipe, wash hands, set out tools, measure, then turn on the heat
Wash hands, turn on the heat, then read the recipe
check.why: Reading, hand washing and setup all come before the heat. Nothing on the stove should be waiting for you.

lessons.title: A Time Plan for a Lab
lessons.mainIdea: Plan a lab backward from the minute it must be done, giving each step a clock time, and start the longest wait first.
reading: A class lab is 45 minutes, and the food has to be eaten and the kitchen clean when the bell rings. That is a puzzle you solve on paper first. Start at the end. Cleanup takes 8 minutes, so cooking must finish at 37 minutes. Eating takes 5, so the food must be on the plate at 32. Now go backward through the recipe: bake 12 minutes, so it goes in the oven at 20; mixing takes 10, so measuring must be done by 10; measuring and setup take 8; hand washing and reading take 2. The plan fits with a few minutes to spare.

Write it as a list with clock times, not just minutes: 9:00 wash hands and read; 9:02 set out tools and measure; 9:10 mix; 9:20 into the oven, start timer; 9:20 to 9:32 wash mixing bowls while it bakes; 9:32 out of the oven, cool 2 minutes, serve; 9:37 cleanup; 9:45 done. That middle line matters. Waiting time is working time. The bowls get washed while the oven does its job, and cleanup at the end is short.

Two rules make the plan work. Start the longest thing first: the oven preheats in the first minute, water for pasta goes on before the vegetables are cut, rice goes on before the stir-fry starts. And give one person one job when you work in a group. One measures dry, one measures wet, one greases the pan and preheats. Nobody stands and watches. If a step runs long, the plan shows you exactly how much you have lost and what to cut, which is usually the last garnish, not the hand washing.

words.d: a written list of each step with the clock time it starts, planned backward from when everything must be done
starting from the finish time and working toward the start to see when each step must begin

look.title: A 45-Minute Muffin Lab
look.cite: example lab plan, muffin recipe with 15-minute bake
look.prompt: Add the minutes. Does the plan fit in 45? What can be done during the 15-minute bake, and what happens to the plan if measuring takes 12 minutes instead of 8?

check.q: A lab is 45 minutes. Cleanup takes 8 and eating takes 5. By what minute must cooking be finished?
check.why: 45 minus 8 for cleanup is 37, and 37 minus 5 for eating is 32. Backward planning starts from the end.

check.q: What is the best use of the 12 minutes while a pan is in the oven?
choices: Sit and wait so nothing is missed
Wash the mixing bowls and wipe the counter
Open the oven every 2 minutes to check
check.why: Waiting time is working time. Cleaning during the bake makes the final cleanup short and the lab finish on time.

check.q: Which should start first in a stir-fry lab: the rice, the vegetable chopping, or the stir-fry?
choices: The stir-fry, since it is the main dish
The chopping, since it uses knives
The rice, because it takes the longest
check.why: Start the longest step first. Rice takes 15 to 20 minutes and cooks by itself while you chop and stir-fry.

lessons.title: When an Ingredient Is Missing
lessons.mainIdea: A substitution swaps a missing ingredient for one that does the same job in the recipe; know the standard swaps and what changes.
reading: The recipe says buttermilk and the refrigerator has plain milk. Do not give up, and do not just pour in milk. A *substitution* is an ingredient that does the same job as the missing one. Buttermilk's job is to be sour, so it reacts with baking soda and makes the batter rise. Put 1 Tbsp of vinegar or lemon juice in a liquid cup, fill to the 1-cup line with milk, and let it stand 5 minutes. It will look curdled. That is right. Use it as the recipe's 1 cup of buttermilk.

A few standard swaps cover most kitchen emergencies. 1 tsp baking powder: use 1/4 tsp baking soda plus 1/2 tsp cream of tartar. 1 oz unsweetened baking chocolate: use 3 Tbsp cocoa powder plus 1 Tbsp butter or oil. 1 cup cake flour: use 1 cup all-purpose flour minus 2 Tbsp. 1 cup sour cream in a batter: plain yogurt, cup for cup. Fresh herbs to dried: use one third as much dried, since drying concentrates them. Write these on the same cabinet door as the equivalents chart.

Some swaps change the result and some do not work at all. Oil for butter in cookies makes them spread more and lose the butter taste. Baking soda for baking powder, measure for measure, will not rise and will taste soapy; they are not the same thing. Sugar cut in half in a cake changes its texture, not just its sweetness. Before you swap, ask what the ingredient does: rise, bind, add fat, add sour, add flavor. Swap for something that does the same job, and expect a small change. Then write on the card what you did and how it came out.

words.d: an ingredient used in place of a missing one because it does the same job in the recipe
a sour milk used in baking; 1 cup can be replaced by 1 Tbsp vinegar or lemon juice plus milk to make 1 cup
a leavening that contains its own acid; 1 tsp can be replaced by 1/4 tsp baking soda plus 1/2 tsp cream of tartar

look.title: Pantry Check
look.text: Pancake recipe: 1 cup buttermilk, 1 egg, 2 Tbsp melted butter, 1 cup flour, 1 Tbsp sugar, 1 tsp baking powder, 1/2 tsp baking soda, 1/4 tsp salt. The refrigerator has plain milk, eggs and butter but no buttermilk. The cabinet has flour, sugar, salt, baking soda, cream of tartar and white vinegar, but the baking powder can is empty.
look.prompt: Make the two substitutions with exact amounts. Which ingredient's job is the buttermilk doing, and why does that make the baking soda in the recipe matter?

check.q: A recipe needs 1 cup of buttermilk. Which substitution works?
choices: 1 cup water with a pinch of salt
1 cup of milk, plain, with nothing added
1 Tbsp vinegar or lemon juice plus milk to make 1 cup, standing 5 minutes
check.why: Buttermilk's job is to be sour. Vinegar or lemon juice in milk does the same job with baking soda.

check.q: The baking powder is gone. A recipe needs 1 tsp. What do you use?
choices: 1/4 tsp baking soda plus 1/2 tsp cream of tartar
check.why: Baking powder is soda plus an acid. Soda alone, measure for measure, does not rise properly and tastes soapy.

check.q: A recipe calls for 1 Tbsp of fresh basil. You have only dried. How much do you use?
check.why: Dried herbs are stronger, so use one third as much. One third of a tablespoon is 1 teaspoon.

review.q: What is the factor for scaling a recipe that serves 8 up to 40?
review.why: 40 divided by 8 is 5. Every ingredient is multiplied by 5.

review.q: A recipe says to fold in the whipped cream. Which tool and motion is right?
choices: A rubber spatula, cutting down and turning over gently
A wooden spoon stirring in circles
review.why: Folding keeps the air in a light mixture. Beating or stirring knocks it out.

review.q: After scaling, a recipe needs 5 tsp of salt. What is the easiest way to measure it?
review.why: 3 tsp = 1 Tbsp, so 5 tsp is 1 Tbsp plus 2 tsp.

review.q: In a 45-minute lab, what should happen during the 15 minutes a dish is baking?
choices: The recipe is read for the first time
The next day's ingredients are measured
The mixing tools are washed and the counter wiped
review.why: Waiting time is working time. Cleaning during the bake keeps the lab on schedule.

review.q: The first read of a recipe, before cooking, turns up: marinate 4 hours. You have 1 hour. What is the right move?
choices: Change plans now, while you can pick a different recipe or a quick marinade
Start cooking and read the rest later
review.why: Hidden time is why you read the whole recipe first. Catching it early gives you choices.

review.q: A recipe for 48 cookies is cut in half. It called for 1 cup of butter. How much butter now?
review.why: Half of 1 cup is 1/2 cup, which is one stick of butter.

review.q: A student adds a pile of chicken pieces to a hot pan all at once and they turn gray and wet. What is the cause?
choices: The oil was the wrong kind
The chicken was cut too small
The pan was crowded, so its temperature dropped and the meat steamed
review.why: Crowding cools the pan. Cook in batches so each piece sears and browns.

review.q: Which is the best description of mise en place?
choices: Cooking everything at once to save time
Reading the recipe after the food is in the pan
Every ingredient measured and prepped and every tool set out before the heat goes on
review.why: Mise en place is the setup before cooking. It keeps your hands free to stir and watch once the pan is hot.
